## **Notes** 

##### Units used: 

Unless otherwise stated, all statistics on platinum and palladium supply and demand are expressed in terms of fine metal content.  All references in this publication to “ounces” refer to troy ounces. 

**One troy ounce =** 31.103 grammes **One tonne =** 32,151 troy ounces **“dollar”** US dollar unless otherwise stated 

##### Prices: 

Unless otherwise stated, US dollars and their equivalents are for the pm fixes of the London Platinum and Palladium Market. 

Terminology: 

Estimates of **supply** _include_ mine production and the recycling of both scrapped autocatalysts and old jewellery but _exclude_ contributions from above-ground stocks, such as supplies from stocks controlled by state institutions in Russia. 

**Demand** estimates are _net_ of recycling with the exception of autocatalyst and jewellery, where _gross_ demand is shown. i.e. the total amount of metal supplied to these two sectors.  Estimates of recycling from scrapped autocatalysts and jewellery are shown separately as part of supply given their scale and potential for change.  (This year’s survey is the second in which we have presented jewellery fabrication as gross with a separate series for scrap; prior to this, jewellery was shown on a net basis.)  Estimates of demand exclude the movements of any above-ground stocks held within the specified industries, for example any changes in stocks held by the automotive industry. 

By simple arithmetic, this leaves either a **“Gross Surplus or Deficit”** before any movements in above-ground stocks are considered.  This is a critical measure of the underlying fundamentals of platinum and palladium and indicates the extent to which fabrication demand may have depended on the release of abo

ve-ground stocks, or otherwise.  At the same time, this also indicates the change in global above-ground stocks. 

Unless otherwise stated, all references to **“above-ground stocks”** of platinum and palladium refer to stocks of refined metal, of a form and quality accepted as good delivery in the Zurich market and the world’s principal commodity exchanges.  Our supply/demand tables also show **“Estimated Movements in Stocks”** .  These specific movements relate only to above-ground stock holdings for which reasonable estimates of movement can be made and attributed. A listing and breakdown of these appears in the more detailed tables in the Appendices section of this Survey. 

Having allowed for the Estimated Movements in Stocks as defined above, the **“Residual Surplus or Deficit”** is arrived at by deduction.  A **residual deficit** implies the extent to which **_other above-ground stocks_** , including those held by financial institutions and/or investors, were released to meet fabrication demand.  Conversely a **residual surplus** implies the extent to which these **_other above-ground stock_** holdings were added to.  However, this should not be construed as indicating the change in global above-ground stocks.  For this, please refer to the reported Gross Surplus or Deficit. 

**Throughout the tables, totals may not add due to independent rounding.**

## **1. Executive Summary** 

As far as platinum and palladium prices are concerned, much has changed since our previous report in June of this year – specifically, over recent weeks since late September.  However, while the current price environment is materially different, our view of the underlying fundamentals is largely unchanged.  After another significant gross surplus this year (0.7m ounces), platinum is expected to remain in surplus for the duration of the forecast period, although the scale of these is expected to ease somewhat in 2013-14. Meanwhile, 2011 should result in a further although reduced gross deficit in palladium (0.34m ounces), with continuing shortfalls anticipated in each of the forecast years thereafter; these being somewhat larger than the level we expect this year.  (Note: these underlying balances exclude stock related activity such as ETF flows and Russian government inventory sales). 

in the all important autocatalyst sector, this being the largest source of demand for both metals.  Dominant in diesel applications, platinum is heavily exposed to Europe; this region being the world’s largest light diesel market and hence the biggest consumer of platinum in autocatalysts.  As well as lacklustre vehicle production in Europe, platinum faces additional headwinds due to the absence of market share growth for light diesels and continuing substitution by palladium.  Therefore, with a lack of momentum from its principal source of demand, platinum’s forecast growth in autocatalyst is entirely due to risin

g demand for heavy duty diesel applications, including the emerging off-road segment. However, exciting as this undoubtedly is, it will not be sufficient to restore platinum’s vibrancy in the autocatalyst sector as a whole, with demand in 2014 still distant from the high of 2007. Inevitably, these underlying balances have a direct impact on above-ground stocks. In the case of platinum, this results in a continuing escalation, while global stocks of palladium (the more abundant of the two) are expected to erode. Using our stock estimates for the end of last year as a reference (3.8m and 11.4m ounces respectively), these predicted balances will elevate above-ground platinum stocks to an estimated 6.5m ounces by the end of 2014, with stocks of palladium declining to a total of 9.6m ounces. Over the longer term, the negative implications of this for platinum are obvious, as are the more positive connotations for palladium. On the whole, these outcomes for platinum and palladium are symptomatic of their relative fortunes Meanwhile, palladium is even more dominant in light gasoline applications (where its strangle-hold is increasing), which comprise the vast majority of global vehicle production. This gives palladium a more diverse geographic footprint, which includes greater exposure to growth markets such as China and the emerging economies where emissions standards are also tightening. Furthermore, demand for palladium is also assisted by continuing substitution gains versus platinum in both diesel and gasoline applications, even though these are expected to slow in comparison with recent years. Consequently, despite the economic woes in Europe and the United States, we expect record high demand for palladium in autocatalysts as early as next year, with further gains anticipated over the rest of the forecast period. However, in the medium term (the next 18 months or so), the overarching climate for precious metals

investment is expected to remain the dominant force as far as prices are concerned. When our last report was released in June, platinum and palladium traded at averages that month of $1,770 and $771 respectively and averaged not far from these levels through to mid-September. From that point, however, amid a widespread sell-off in commodities and equities, platinum touched a near two year low of $1,442 in early October trading, with palladium sinking to $549 – its lowest level in more than a year. Although both have since managed something of an improvement, this has been hesitant and lacking in conviction thus far, with prices still well adrift of recent levels. In the main, the causes of this sell-off were centred on the deepening sovereign debt crisis in the eurozone and the associated squeeze on liquidity. Amid intense anxiety pending a credible plan to manage a default by Greece, recapitalise the region’s banks and prevent further contagion (and indeed, save the euro!), the economic recovery in Europe has stalled and the danger of sliding back into recession is mounting. Meanwhile, the recovery in the US has also lost momentum in the face of continuing high unemployment and a depressed housing market, with already weak consumer confidence having been further dented by the recent debt-ceiling fiasco. By late September, in the midst of this turmoil, action from the Fed to help revive a flagging US economy turned out to be a reprise of “Operation Twist” from the 1960s (a measure to curb long-term interest rates). This policy choice was preferred over a third round of quantitative easing which, given its inflationary implications, would have been very favourable for precious metals (gold in particular) had it occurred. As it turned out, with liquidity drying up, amid rising anxiety over eurozone exposures, this preference against printing more money, sparked fears of an impending cash-crunch similar to that seen in late 2008, triggering the sell-off of riskier assets and a flight to cash. While brutal for platinum and palladium (with gold taking big hits as well), this has thus far proved much less extreme than the bail-out of late 2008. On the demand side of the equation, platinum’s slide has been arrested by positive responses from jewellery fabrication in China and retail investment in Japan, helped in both cases by platinum being less expensive than gold (an exceptionally rare event). Meanwhile, unlike the situation in 2008, the cost of mine production in South Africa (of which there is greater awareness) appears to have come into play much earlier than before, encouraging bargain-hunting investors back into platinum and helping to support prices. While this support may be attributable in part to South African mine economics as well, palladium’s re-engagement with investors is most likely due to its promising underlying fundamentals and the anticipated conclusion before long of Russian government inventory sales. With their recent losses now stemmed, we believe that platinum and palladium prices will enter a period of rehabilitation over the remainder of this year, regaining some but not all of their recent losses. For 2011 as a whole, we forecast average prices of $1,733 and $745 respectively; these in fact being record highs, despite a much weaker fourth quarter. This partial recovery in the short term owes much to the continuing uncertainties over eurozone policy and the prospects for economic growth in Europe and the US next year. In contrast, we are considerably more positive about gold, which we expect to quickly recoup its recent losses before going on to thrive next year in a volatile atmosphere of latent uncertainty. Indeed in our base case assumptions, we see gold peaking in 2012, with prices trading frequently above $2,000 over the latter part of next year. While such a climate may not be entirely conducive for platinum and palladium (due to their demand base in autocatalyst and industrial applications), we believe they will find renewed investor interest in this environment, with supply-side economics continuing to feature prominently. Consequently, we expect somewhat stronger average prices in 2012 than those we anticipate this year, and forecast averages of $1,763 and $819 respectively. However, these gains are slender by comparison with the much stronger performance we expect from gold next year and are tempered by continuing uncertainties in the broader economy, especially in Europe and the US. Therefore, as a consequence of gold’s anticipated strength next year, we expect platinum prices on average to remain below gold throughout 2012 and most likely into early 2013. This should be supportive of platinum jewellery demand next year, even though average platinum prices are expected to return to elevated levels. Looking forward to 2013, this is the year in which we expect the bull market in gold to begin to dissipate, especially in the se

cond half of the year. We see this as symptomatic of the eventual resolution of many of the high profile financial problems the world currently faces, the emergence of sustainable economic growth and a move towards positive real interest rates in western economies. While such conditions may initially appear favourable for both platinum and palladium, this will inevitably usher in a period of heavy investor selling, led by the significant liquidation of positions in gold. Given platinum’s traditionally strong relationship with gold, we expect it to suffer more in this period than palladium, weighed down by its continuing gross surplus and swollen above-ground stocks. Meanwhile, although palladium may suffer some collateral damage, we believe investors will be more inclined to maintain their exposure, given what should by then be increasingly attractive fundamentals and with Russian government sales all but over. We forecast average prices in 2013 of $1,688 and $848 for platinum and palladium respectively, these denoting a material contraction in the price differential between them. ## **2. Economic Assumptions** 

#### **2.1 Introduction** 

Thomson Reuters GFMS’ views for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios, namely the Base Case Scenario, Scenario B and Scenario C.  Under our **Base Case** , we expect a slowdown in the world GDP growth this and next year.  This is mainly driven by persistent sovereign debt crises, fiscal policy tightening and a slowdown in industrial production in major advanced economies. Although developing world countries continue to expand, global growth is likely to moderate due to tight monetary policies in a number of countries and downward pressure on external demand stemming from economic and financial problems in industrialised countries.  However, we expect global growth to improve gradually over the final two years of our forecast which is mainly driven by emerging markets. We view this as the most likely scenario with a 45% probability. 

Our more bullish **Scenario B** with a 40% probability predicts a global economic recovery with higher growth rates in the major advanced and developing countries over the forecast period.  Under this scenario, we assume that the US government and the Federal Reserve continue to implement loose fiscal and monetary policies.  As a consequence, we expect negative real interest rates and rising inflation, with the latter reaching an annual average of 5.8% in 2014. Moreover, the US dollar weakens under this scenario.  It is of note that we have raised the possibility of Scenario B by 10% since our June forecast, reflecting increasing concerns over the sovereign debt problem on both sides of the Atlantic over the last couple of months. 

Under our bearish **Scenario C** , to which we assign a 15% probability (down by 5% from the previous report), we expect the effect of government measures to be negligible on the longer run growth rate as the global economy struggles to escape deflation. Consequently, global GDP growth slows appreciably in 2011 and remains sluggish over much of the rest of the forecast period, particularly in the developed world. 

The sections below start by describing the background to the current economic situation.  We then discuss in more detail each of the three economic scenarios with a particular focus on some individual countries. 

#### **2.2 Economic Backdrop** 

Growing concerns over the sovereign debt problem in both Europe and the United States not only undermined the stability of banking syst

ems and financial markets, but also raised worries regarding a potential slowdown in the world economy. Indeed, the IMF cut its predictions for GDP growth in Europe for the next two years. The outlook for Greece remains the worst as its economy is expected to contract for four successive years. Furthermore, Italy’s credit rating has been recently downgraded by Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s, and Fitch on the back of its weakening growth prospects and structural economic problems. Similarly, Spanish government debt has been recently downgraded by all major credit rating agencies due to growing concerns about the country’s ability to cut its debt and about its growth prospects. As the European sovereign debt crisis intensifies, equity investors are becoming more reluctant to provide liquidity, putting pressure on European banks and the real economy. As a result, the shares of European banks have fallen by 40% over the last three months. The price of Credit Default Swaps (CDS), a type of insurance against default, also rose, as the banks are struggling to obtain funding. The situation in Europe remains very complex and it is still very difficult to predict the outcome of the Eurozone debt problem. One of the possible solutions could be a rapid shift to a full fiscal union. This would put the Eurozone gross government debt to still high but manageable level. Nevertheless, we regard this as a very unlikely outcome as the member states would be highly reluctant to give up their fiscal independence. #### **2.3 Base Case Scenario** 

Real **global** GDP growth is expected to ease back to 2.8% this year, having rebounded to 5.1% in 2010. This is due to the indebted nature of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world. Meanwhile, further tightening of monetary policies in emerging markets to fight surging inflation will also slow down world GDP growth this year.  Next year, we expect a further decline in global GDP growth, an annual average of 2.5% due to a deterioration in the European sovereign debt problem.  This is followed by faster growth in 2013 and 2014 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending and the property market, start to improve.  Both will be aided by unemployment beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels. 

While **US** GDP growth for the second quarter of this year has been recently revised up to 1.3% from the 

preliminary estimate of 1.0%, the economic recovery remains fragile.  Central to this is ongoing weakness in consumer spending, which accounts for some 70% of American economic activity.  Meanwhile, it also reflects a continuation of an elevated unemployment rate coupled with a lacklustre property market, both of which are likely to remain in place for an extended period.  Indeed, facing a major slowdown in economic growth, the Federal Reserve has already confirmed that it would like to keep interest rates unchanged until mid-2013.  Furthermore, a new stimulus plan known as “Operation Twist” has been recently announced.  Under this, the Fed will buy $400 billion of long-term Treasury bonds by next June, while selling an equivalent amount of shorter-term securities.  The plan is designed to lower long-term interest rates, while keeping shortterm rates little changed. 

Nevertheless, as interest rates have already been cut to record lows, we doubt this new measure of monetary stimulus will be effective to restore consumer confidence and boost GDP growth.  Although our base case scenario does not assume that the US economy will fall back into recession next year, the downside risk is growing, particularly given the persistence of elevated unemployment, weakness in the housing market and deeper contagion from the European sover

eign debt crisis. As a result, US GDP growth is expected to slow further to 1.5% in 2012 (compared with 2.0% in our previous report) before economic conditions slowly improve from 2013 onwards. Our GDP forecast for the **EU-27** has been revised lower since the previous forecast, as growth in Germany and France, the two largest economies in the Eurozone, both stalled in the second quarter. Looking back at Chinese platinum jewellery fabrication over the last decade, we can see extraordinary swings in

After reaching a peak of 1.67M ounces in 2002, offtake halved to no more than 835,000 ounces four years later, before rebounding strongly in late 2008 to then achieve a seven-year high of just above 1.6M ounces in 2009.  Thereafter, however, demand fell back last year, dropping by 26% to less than 1.2M ounces. 

The key factor behind this dramatic change in jewellery fabrication has been the trend in platinum prices, as a massive increase in prices in the middle part of the 2000s saw the competition from more affordable white K-Gold and palladium jewellery impact platinum’s market share.  Not surprisingly, after the collapse of the platinum price in late 2008, demand immediately recovered, on the back of greater price attractiveness to consumers as well as an improvement in the jewellery trade’s profit margins. 

The price sensitivity of platinum jewellery demand is also clear from intra-year developments in 2011. During the first eight months of this year, against a backdrop of elevated platinum prices, demand remained broadly flat year-on-year. In contrast, following the steep correction in platinum prices in the second half of September, output has since recovered strongly.  For example, turnover on the Shanghai Gold Exchange 

(the only official source of VAT-free platinum in China) posted its highest monthly figure in September. Meanwhile, our latest information from various trade sources suggests that unofficial flows of platinum from Hong Kong to mainland China have also picked up over the last few weeks.
